suggestions.assertion: The response explicitly names the overlapping existing skill (soma-agent-debugger)
suggestions.reason: In isolation this assertion is weak — a response that named soma-agent-debugger while giving a wrong or fabricated justification for the overlap would still satisfy it. It only becomes discriminating in this eval because expectation 3 forces genuine reasoning about the match; if expectation 3 were ever dropped, expectation 2 alone would not catch a superficial 'I see a skill with a similar name so I won't build one' response.

No assertion checks that the executor was transparent about the limits of its own check — recommendation.md explicitly flags that it compared only against the catalog description, not the real soma-agent-debugger SKILL.md body, and states what would change the recommendation if that turns out to be inaccurate. This is a real quality signal (honesty about verification depth) that the current expectations don't reward or require, so a future run that fabricated having 'confirmed' the real skill's modes would pass all three current expectations just as easily as this honest one did.

eval_feedback.overall: The three expectations are solid as a set, with expectation 3 doing the real discriminating work: it specifically forces the model to recognize soma-agent-debugger as operational/mode-based rather than defaulting to the more common knowledge-base references/ patch, and the output clearly earns that pass with a dedicated section reasoning through the distinction correctly against the real skill-distiller SKILL.md text. Expectation 2 is comparatively weak on its own but is adequately backstopped by expectation 3. Consider adding an assertion around honesty/calibration (the model should flag, not fabricate, when it can't verify the matched skill's actual internal structure) since that behavior was present here but isn't currently required.
